{ id: 'prism_complete', kind: 'thm', kname: null, ktitle: 'complete original prism theorem', parent: 't_prismd', title: 'Prism with one diagonal: seven original trees cover every case', status: 'proved', statement: `Every convex realization of this face type unfolds along original edges. Six near-stars and one triangular-chain tree suffice. All curvature equalities are included.`, explanation: `This completes the repository’s written argument for all seven six-vertex types. Independent mathematical review and formal verification have not been performed. Numerical experiments are not proof premises.`, body: `

The simple finite rule

Try the three trees obtained by cutting all four edges at vertex 1 and then 52, 53, or 54. Also try the three trees at vertex 3 with fifth cut 20, 21, or 25. The seventh candidate cuts 02, 12, 25, 35, 45. Every cut is an original edge.

The proof shows that at least one of these seven candidates always succeeds. It explains how failure of the first proof test forces a successful switch, rather than relying on a finite search over shapes.

Four cases cover every shape

Curvature caseWhy a candidate works
Every vertex ≤180°The existing flat-hinge theorem chooses an original near-star, including equality.
Vertex 2 or 5 is sharpA sharp-slit near-star works, or three angle identities force the seventh tree to work.
Both fans low; vertex 0 or 4 sharpUse the other source. If its middle triangle is obtuse, the corresponding middle angle in the fallback is acute, so that fallback works.
Only an original source 1 or 3 is sharpTry its three permitted weighted cuts. If all tests fail, their curvature sums force the alternate-source conditions from the preceding case.

Why the seventh tree is a useful fallback

Its triangular faces form one connected chain. That chain has exactly the same placement as part of a known nonoverlapping shortest-path star. Thus 14 of its 15 face pairs are always safe. Only the two quadrilaterals need to be separated.

The last forced switch

Suppose source 1 is sharp, but all three original fifth-cut tests fail. The failures at endpoints 3 and 4 imply κ3+κ4+κ5<180°. Since total curvature is 720°, κ0+κ1+κ2>540°. A genuine vertex has curvature below 360°, so κ0+κ2>180°. The other required condition, κ0+κ1>180°, follows from source 1 being sharp.

Those two inequalities allow source 3 with fifth cut 20. If its one remaining pair is Case B, it is safe. If its middle angle is at most 90°, it is safe by the wider Case A lemma. If that middle angle is obtuse, another angle in the same triangle is acute; the seventh tree then has a safe view of its two quadrilaterals. Reflection handles source 3.

What is complete, and what still needs work?

No existence branch remains open among the seven six-vertex types in this written argument. The next essential step is independent mathematical review of the dependency chain. These are research proofs, not a claim of community acceptance or formal verification.

The stronger every-slit Lemma F and the old fixed two-tree minus-edge conjecture remain open. They are optional strengthenings of the completed existence argument.

Proofs and reproducible exact checks

Complete exhaustive prism proof · Sharp-fan switch and its three angle identities · The alternate-source gate switch · Exact rational coefficient audit of all three identities · Independent seven-candidate net checks on former failures and full parameter families · The critical sharp-fan angle switch, throughout a nine-parameter family · The obtuse-to-acute gate switch, throughout a nine-parameter family.

The angle audit proves identities of indeterminates subject to the exact face-angle sums. Positivity and geometric implications are explained in the written proofs. The examples are separate checks, not a finite substitute for the universal argument.

` },

{ id: 't_prismd', kind: 'thm', kname: null, ktitle: 'prism with one diagonal', statement: `Every convex realization of this prism-with-one-diagonal type has a nonoverlapping original-edge unfolding among seven specified trees.`, parent: 'n6', title: 'Prism with one diagonal', status: 'proved', icon: 'prismd', deg: '4·4·3·3·3·3, faces 3⁴ 4²', summary: `Complete written proof: six near-stars and one triangular-chain fallback cover every curvature case. Independent review pending.`, leadFigure: 't_prismd', statementHeading: 'The complete written theorem', afterStatement: `

Read the complete proof and seven-candidate rule. This closes the seventh six-vertex type as a written research argument, pending independent mathematical review. Both quadrilaterals remain whole.

The proposed reduction, retained as history

The old limit argument required nearby octahedral nets to avoid both added diagonals. The new proof chooses original-edge trees directly and supplies its own exhaustive switches.

`, figureHeading: 'A different shape: the two-pair tree can fail', figure: 'prism_failure', body: `

The new full proof covers every curvature branch and equality case. The example above still refutes the single fixed two-pair tree; it does not refute the seven-candidate theorem.

The triangular-chain reduction proves 14 of 15 pairs in that fallback universally. The remaining quadrilateral pair is safe when the other candidate's proof test fails.

Earlier prism progress and counterexamples, retained as history

Latest proof map: every three-sharp-vertex pattern is now covered, and most two-sharp pairs are covered. The new star comparison explains what remains to check. The full types stay open.

New complete branch: if the end vertices 2 and 5 both have curvature at least 180°, the two-pair tree always works. All 15 face pairs are proved safe, including equality. Other high-curvature shapes remain open.

Previous continuation: new original-edge curvature budgets and exact failures of the simplest fallback. The sharp-slit reduction isolates at most two remaining opposite-petal checks, in Case A. This entire type remains open.

New geometric family: this entire type has an original-edge unfolding whenever all curvatures are at most 180°. The proof keeps every artificial diagonal uncut. Maximum curvature strictly above 180° remains open in general; additional fixed-tree families are proved there too. The older coordinate-box and candidate-rule results below retain their own scopes.

The direct nine-parameter model preserves both original quadrilaterals. The tree with only two residual pairs fails on this exactly checked integer-coordinate example: Q1 and Q3 overlap after unfolding.

What this says about Reduction 1. This example refutes the claim that the displayed fixed tree always works. Reduction 1 is a conditional limit argument: it requires successful unfoldings of approaching simplicial refinements that leave both added diagonals uncut. A single failed tree does not refute that implication. In fact, another original-edge tree is exactly certified to unfold this same polyhedron without overlap. The hypothesis needed to apply the reduction to every shape remains unproved.

The failing cuts are ca, cb, cc′, c′a′, c′b′. A certified successful alternative uses ca, ab, bb′, cc′, c′a′. See the overlap certificate and successful alternative.

A larger explicit region now has an independently verified cover of 443 subregions using three trees. A separate search box, centered on a different shape, still has 94 unresolved regions; the universal case remains open. These are closed boxes of shapes, not 443 sample polyhedra: all shapes in the specified box are certified, including its boundary.

Which prism-with-one-diagonal shapes are covered?

Use c=(0,0,0), a=(1,0,0), b=(x,y,0), c′=(u,v,w), a′=A a+B c′, b′=C b+D c′. The parameter order is (x,y,u,v,w,A,B,C,D); the center is (−3,1/10,−3,0,1,4,1/2,1,1). The respective half-widths are (1/10,1/100,1/10,1/100,1/10,1/10,3/100,3/100,3/100). Vary every parameter independently within those bounds.

Latest investigation: two routes around a quadrilateral

A vertex of degree four is missing just one of the other vertices. They lie at opposite corners of a quadrilateral. After cutting the four edges at this vertex, there are two ways to connect the missing corner by following the quadrilateral boundary. Repeating this at the other degree-four vertex gives four candidate trees.

What is now ruled out: both routes can fail if we commit to one fixed apex. In another exact example, choosing the sharper degree-four apex and then taking the shorter boundary route also fails, while its longer route succeeds. Shorter cuts do not necessarily put the unfolded faces in safer positions.

What remains worth trying: choose the sharper degree-four apex but keep both routes available. A numerical search of 60,000 shapes found no failure of that pair. This is a conjectural selection rule, not a proof. The universal prism-with-one-diagonal case stays open.

Exact route examples and checks

The shorter-route example has a=(50,0,0), b=(−5,10,0), c=(0,0,0), a′=(−4,0,24), b′=(−39,1,11), c′=(−35,0,10). Exact comparisons show that a′ is sharper than b. The shorter route a′–c′–c produces overlap; the longer a′–a–c has a simple net. Full explanation and reproduction instructions · exact verification report.

See the chart and failure witnesses and the exact coverage bounds.

` },

{ id: 'tidy_proof', parent: 'root', title: 'The streamlined proof — review in progress', status: 'info', summary: 'A complete shorter draft, with every original proof and alternative preserved.', body: `

The separate draft now runs from the graph classification through all three remaining geometric proofs. This is a further self-audit; independent mathematical review is still pending. The original notes, figures, failures and alternative approaches remain available.

Read the streamlined proof · Read the shared geometric details · Review record.

What has become shorter?

  1. The classification: an elementary graph-complement argument leaves four types without a vertex joined to all the others. A dome theorem settles the ordinary prism, leaving the three geometric arguments here.
  2. Local separation: each flattened patch spans less than half the fan angle under the relevant source conditions. This replaces the separate one-sided spherical-link estimate.
  3. The finite cut edges: one hypothetical-crossing obstruction combines the two source-curvature proofs.
  4. The small-fan region: the middle blue triangle itself rules out the wrong interior of the auxiliary curve. A single curvature contradiction then handles both source branches.
  5. The last four pairs: a short boundary table replaces the old interior-hinge reduction.
  6. The minus-edge switch: one positive-sum identity replaces four angle comparisons.
  7. The prism switches: two views of the same fallback net supply one shared observation. Shorter exact angle identities force the required switch.

What is being checked?

The main review targets are the containment and six-sided-region arguments, the applicability to whole quadrilaterals, and equality in each selection test. The seven new automated checks pass: they check exact identities, the finite graph classification, explicit half-fan domains, and the necessary inequalities on a real historical overlap. Read the exact check report. These checks do not formally verify the universal geometric proof.

How this relates to the yellow lemmas

The selected Lemma F and selected Triple Lemma are green. Their stronger every-slit forms remain optional yellow questions and are not needed by this existence proof.

Earlier draft and retained source files

The first draft contained the half-fan, finite-cut, small-fan and minus-edge simplifications while the full dependency chain was still being assembled. That chain is now written in the separate presentation above and remains under review.

Editable proof source · Editable geometric core · Original complete dependency map. No earlier research material has been removed.

` },
